purpose: Pattern library abstracted from 3 IFOLOGY FILMS hits. Used by docs/story/STORY_BLUEPRINT.md (writing) and docs/story/IDEA_ENGINE.md (idea scoring). Evidence points at data/story/transcripts and data/story/beats. Quotes are evidence only (10 words max) and must never be reused in scripts.

sources.title: What IF You Could Stop Time?

hook.name: Mundane problem, instant power fix
hook.description: The video opens mid-scene, with no intro or title card, on a tiny everyday problem (late, spill, mix-up) that the power solves in one visible move. Second person, present tense, with the first word inside the action. It lasts 11-35 s.

evidence.note: 1 minute until the bell; seated before it rings.
Juice frozen mid-fall in a frozen cafeteria; you scoop it back.
Two identical moms in the kitchen; dad runs a test.

hook.reuse: Pick a 5-second annoyance from a 13-25-year-old's day (alarm, bus, homework, sibling, phone at 1%). Show the power fix it in one shot. Never open on the power doing something heroic: open small and save scale for later.

hook.name: Witness who missed it
hook.description: The cold open ends on a bystander who saw the result but not the power. They ask a short confused question, and you or the narrator answer deadpan. The viewer feels in on the secret (dramatic irony) before the premise has even been stated.

evidence.note: Classmate asks if you just left.
Friend asks about a spill that no longer exists.
Dad asks both moms a question only mom would know.

hook.reuse: End the cold open on a 3-8 word confused line from a witness (friend, parent, teacher) plus a 2-5 word deadpan answer. Then cut straight to the title question.

hook.name: Cold open seeds the rules
hook.description: Odd details in the cold open are explained later as rules or problems, which gives a 'that's why' click minutes later. In Shapeshift the kid voice becomes Rule 3 and its climax payoff, and the barking dog becomes Problem 2. In Stop Time, scooping the juice demonstrates Rule 2 before the rule is stated.

evidence.note: The kid voice is explained at 3:12 and paid off when you nail an adult voice at 16:00.
The dog barks only at you; dogs smell the real you.
The juice moves only while you hold it (Rule 2).

hook.reuse: Put 1-2 visible oddities in the cold open that you do not explain. Explain them in the rules or costs section, and if possible use one of them in the climax.

hook.name: Object close-up first frame
hook.description: The first shot is a close-up of a concrete object that signals time or the problem (an alarm clock at 7:59, a cafeteria tray, a kitchen spatula). The first 30 s use fast cuts: 25 shots in the first 60 s of 10x Faster, and 43.6 cuts/min in its cold open.

evidence.note: Hook contact sheet opens on a red alarm clock reading 7:59.
The cold open is the fastest-cut beat of the episode (43.6 cuts/min).

hook.frequency: 3/3 open on an object or close-up
hook.reuse: Shot 1 is a prop close-up that states the problem with no words (a clock, a phone at 1%, a test score). Cut every 1.5-3 s until the title card.

title_question.name: Verbatim title question, then mechanism pivot
title_question.description: The exact title question is spoken as a 'So, what if...' line between 0:11 and 0:36, the moment the cold open's button lands. The next sentence is always the 'here is how it works' pivot. On screen, the title card sits over an in-world 3D establishing shot (suburb aerial, a wall clock, a hallway), not over a plain background.

evidence.note: Title card over an aerial suburb.
Title card over the cafeteria wall clock.
Title card over a hallway transformation shimmer.

title_question.reuse: Say the title word for word by 0:40 at the latest, and earlier (around 0:15) if the cold open is a single gag. Overlay the title card on a wide establishing shot of the episode's main set. Vary the pivot wording each episode, but always state that the mechanism comes next.

title_question.name: Scope widening second question
title_question.description: An optional second question that widens what is possible (from 'anyone' to 'anything'). It promises variety in the perk montage.

evidence.note: Widens from people to objects.

title_question.reuse: Use it when the power has a hidden second dimension (objects as well as people, past as well as future). Keep it to one sentence.

mechanism.name: What changes / what stays the same
mechanism.description: The mechanism is stated in 2-4 plain sentences that name exactly which part of you changes, then explicitly what stays normal. The thing that stays normal is the planted limit and becomes the main problem later.

evidence.note: The legs change; the eyes, brain and reflexes stay normal and are flagged as important.
Bones slide, face folds, 3 seconds, feels like a stretch.

mechanism.reuse: Write it in this order: [body part or system] changes by [number]. Everything else is normal, especially [limit]. Flag the limit with a short 'keep this in mind' signal, worded freshly each time.

mechanism.name: One-line teaser before each science fact
mechanism.description: Each fact is announced as weird, crazy or real before it is given. This opens a 1-2 sentence curiosity gap and stops the explainer from feeling like a lecture.

evidence.note: A 'something weird first' teaser before the clock illusion.
'Crazy part' and then 'weird part' before the cuttlefish facts.
'This part is real' before the cheetah facts.

mechanism.reuse: Before every science anchor, add a 3-6 word teaser that labels the fact (weird, real, the part nobody expects). Never use the same teaser twice in an episode.

mechanism.name: Real-world precedent anchor
mechanism.description: 1-3 true facts show that a small version of the power already exists in nature, the body or technology: sprinter ground-contact research, the stopped-clock illusion, GPS relativity, fly vision, cuttlefish, face recognition. Each is credited loosely ('scientists tested', a named university, a record holder).

evidence.note: Treadmill ground-contact study.
Three anchors in 44 s: illusion, GPS, fly.
Cuttlefish, then the number of faces a person knows.

mechanism.reuse: Find a precedent of the form 'a [animal/organ/machine] already does a tiny version of this'. Give one checkable number. Credit a plausible source type. Verify every fact before writing it.

mechanism.name: Normal-vs-you number ladder
mechanism.description: A normal baseline number becomes 'now it's N', followed by 2-4 escalating comparisons the viewer can picture (highway car, race car, world-record holder, record time).

evidence.note: 25 to 250 km/h, then car, race car, the fastest sprinter, and a 100 m time.

mechanism.reuse: For any multiplier power: baseline (an ordinary teen) -> you -> 3 comparisons in rising order -> a beat-the-record line. Put a speedometer or HUD overlay on a 3D shot while it is narrated.

mechanism.name: Physics breaks it, rules repair it
mechanism.description: Before the fun, the narrator shows that the naive version of the power would be lethal or useless (with time stopped, light and sound stop and air turns solid). The story then invents rules that fix each problem. This shows rigour and earns trust for the fantasy.

evidence.note: Blind, deaf and stuck, then Rule 1 (a bubble around you) fixes all three.

mechanism.frequency: 1/3 explicit; implicit in Shapeshift (you keep your weight)
mechanism.reuse: Ask what would literally happen. Turn the 2-3 deal-breakers into rules, each with a quick test scene.

limits_costs.name: Flagged plant, flagged callback
limits_costs.description: A limit is planted in the first 30 s with an explicit 'this matters later' flag. It is paid off 3-4 minutes later with a callback that reuses the plant's key words ('your eyes stay normal').

evidence.note: Plant and payoff are 4 minutes apart.

limits_costs.frequency: 2/3 explicit ('remember' appears 2x in 10x Faster and 5x in Shapeshift)
limits_costs.reuse: Use one flagged plant per episode, no more. The callback must reuse the plant's keyword so viewers feel the click.

limits_costs.name: Numbered rules, each demonstrated
limits_costs.description: There are 3-4 enumerated rules. Each one is a statement, then a physical test, then a comic consequence. Rules are discovered by trying things rather than handed over by a mentor.

evidence.note: Rule 1 bubble, Rule 2 touch (basketball and rain test), Rule 3 your minutes are real (book, pizza, nap).
Rules 1-4: weight, study, look-not-skill, don't forget your face.

limits_costs.frequency: 2/3 numbered rules; 10x Faster uses one implicit rule
limits_costs.reuse: Use 3 rules, max 4. Each gets one 10-25 s demo scene with a gag, and at least 2 of them must be used in the climax.

limits_costs.name: Numbered problems: number + gag + cheap fix
limits_costs.description: After the 'but' turn come 3-4 enumerated problems. Each one is: name -> real number -> 2-4 vivid bodily consequences -> a low-tech workaround that looks silly but works -> a family or friend reaction. They are ordered from annoying to expensive to dangerous.

evidence.note: Air (a 100x drag square law, fixed with goggles), shoes (a week per pair), food (14,000 kcal).
Weight, dogs (300 million vs 6 million smell sensors), details (fingerprints), identity.

limits_costs.reuse: Each problem gets a concrete number and a physical gag the engine can show. The fix must be ordinary (goggles, spikes, a photo in your pocket), never a new power.

limits_costs.name: The real problem (a turn inside the costs)
limits_costs.description: After the list of costs, the narrator says none of them is the real problem. The real one is a different kind: physical danger to others (stopping), time debt and loneliness (ageing alone), or losing yourself (forgetting your own face). It lands at 43-50% of a 10-min video.

evidence.note: Stopping, not speed.
Extra lived time adds up; fear of being stuck forever.
Introduced as the problem nobody warned you about.

limits_costs.reuse: Escalate the kind of cost, not just its size: inconvenient -> expensive -> dangerous to others -> existential. The real problem should be the planted limit (L1) or the theme (L7).

limits_costs.name: Chekhov density: every rule fires
limits_costs.description: Almost every rule, gag object and limit returns later. Counted plant-to-payoff pairs: 10x Faster 6, Stop Time 6, Shapeshift 8. The climax is solved with knowledge, not raw power.

evidence.note: The 300 m braking distance becomes the exact braking point in the rescue.
Keeping your weight lets you go flat as a tarp against crushing gravity.
The ice cream you saved is contrasted with the car you don't save.

limits_costs.reuse: Keep a plant ledger while outlining. Every plant needs a payoff, and the climax must cash at least 3.

limits_costs.name: Mastery through borrowed nature
limits_costs.description: The fix for the real problem comes from a real animal or a principle from school (cheetah claws and tail; a flat shape spreads weight). It is learned in a short montage with friends, and it gives a better technique, not a new power.

evidence.note: Cheetah analogy, then spikes, leaning practice and a danger map.
A science-class principle used in the middle of the fight.

limits_costs.reuse: Find the animal or engineering principle that solves the real problem. Show it on a navy card, then give the training montage 2-3 quick tries, with one failure.

limits_costs.name: Theme stated as a practical rule
limits_costs.description: The theme is not a moral speech. It is a usable rule ('slow down before you need to', 'the outside is easy, the inside is hard'), and the climax proves it. Stop Time flips this: its rule is a temptation (nobody can see you), and the climax proves the cost of believing it.

evidence.note: A braking rule doubles as the episode's theme.
Copying the outside of a person versus the inside.
The 'nobody can see you' logic drives the slide.

limits_costs.reuse: Write the theme as an instruction the hero could put on a sticky note. Plant it at 50-65%, and make the climax its proof (or its tragic violation).

escalation.name: Scale ladder
escalation.description: The setting widens every 30-90 s: home -> school -> town -> region or public -> secret organisation or world. No setting repeats at the same scale except as a bookend.

evidence.note: Bedroom, school, track, town deliveries, another city, a street crisis, going viral, the van team, the highway.
Kitchen, hallway, school, zoo, park going viral, city search, garage, a 70,000-seat stadium.

escalation.reuse: List the episode's sets in ladder order before writing. Engine sets map cleanly: bedroom/home -> classroom -> suburb/park -> city/rooftop -> stadium/void.

escalation.name: Stakes curve: flat, then a cliff
escalation.description: Stakes (rated 1-5) stay at 1 for the first 25-45% and rise to 2-3 in the costs. They jump to 5 at the crisis and stay there through the climax and cliffhanger. 10x Faster: stakes 1 until 2:41, 3 at 4:24, 5 at 6:31. Stop Time: 3 at 5:04, 5 at 7:37. Shapeshift: 3 at 6:28, 5 at 7:14.

evidence.note: Each video's stakes curve is stored per beat.

escalation.reuse: The first third should be fun, not tense. Don't fake danger early; the contrast is what makes the crisis land. Keep stakes at 5 for no more than 25% of runtime.

escalation.name: Perk montage scales up and goes public
escalation.description: Perks are ordered personal -> social -> commercial or sport -> long-range. Each is 10-35 s with a button, and the montage ends at the largest perk.

evidence.note: Chores, a pizza job, soccer, lunch in another city.
Queue, test, sleep, soccer, a kindness, a prank.

escalation.reuse: Use 4-6 perks: home chore, school, a job or money, sport or game, one kindness to plant the moral benchmark, and one big-scale flex.

escalation.name: For a while it works... then one day
escalation.description: A one-sentence time compression, then a specific day. This bridges Act 2 into the crisis at 56-63% of a 10-min video (33% in the 22-min one).

evidence.note: A specific weekday plus a place.
'Keep it small' then 'until...'.
A specific day at school.

escalation.reuse: Use exactly one compression line, then name a day and place. Never drift into the crisis with 'and then'.

escalation.name: Moral slide ladder (anti-hero variant)
escalation.description: Instead of a rescue, the power corrupts in rungs, each justified by the same logic: payback, a small theft, a bigger theft, a heist, and finally choosing not to save someone. A best friend acts as the conscience and drifts away.

evidence.note: Snack, shoes, phone, cash truck, then the crash left unfixed.

escalation.reuse: Use it for powers that are hard to detect (invisibility, time, mind). Plant a kindness benchmark in the perk montage, and make the dark choice its mirror image.

escalation.name: Going public summons the bigger world
escalation.description: A viral clip or news story is the hinge from the personal story to the organisation. The world noticing is a consequence of the climax, not a coincidence.

evidence.note: A rescue clip goes viral, then a knock at the door that night.
2 million views, then a van 3 days later.
News footage, then a watcher in a van.

escalation.reuse: End the climax with a public artefact (a clip with an ironic title, a headline, CCTV) and cut to who is watching it.

characters.name: Best friend: witness, translator, conscience
characters.description: A peer who sees the power and names it with a pop-culture reference. They react in lines of 8 words or fewer and become the emotional stake or the moral mirror later (helping with training, doubting you, or being taken).

evidence.note: Names the anime power, then asks if it's bad stuff, then texts about the news.
Milo has his own small power and is abducted (the want).
Friends build the danger-corner map.

characters.reuse: Give the friend one tic (gamer slang, a pet theory) and one arc beat: help, doubt or be endangered. In a 10-min episode the friend gets 3-5 lines.

characters.name: Mom: deadpan reaction and the first to notice the cost
characters.description: Mom reacts to the logistics (shoe count, soaked clothes, cereal size, the moved mug) and is the first to notice the real cost (you look tired; that's not your chin). She closes the arc with a grounding one-liner.

evidence.note: Shoes, cereal, then a dinner blessing.
Soaked, coffee, tired.
Notices the wrong chin.

characters.reuse: Mom gets 2-4 one-line reactions. One of them must spot the hidden cost before the hero admits it.

characters.name: Skeptic authority in the proof test
characters.description: A coach, teacher or principal measures or catches you, does a double-take, and demands a rerun or gets suspicious. This is the external proof, played for comedy.

evidence.note: Whistle, stopwatch, looks up, demands a rerun.
Teacher notes a perfect score again.
Fake principal meets the real one.

characters.reuse: One authority per episode, with a measurable test (stopwatch, scale, exam, camera). Show the triple look (instrument, you, instrument).

characters.name: The innocent: moral test object
characters.description: A small child or ordinary bystander whose safety defines the climax: a kid chasing a ball, a kid with an ice cream, a terrified driver, a stadium crowd.

evidence.note: Kid and ball.
Kid's ice cream vs a crashing driver.

characters.reuse: Plant the innocent's category early (a small kindness in the perk montage), then put a member of that category in danger at the crisis.

characters.name: Ambiguous mentor / recurring stranger
characters.description: A calm adult from an organisation who has been watching you. They appear in the last 25% and are morally unclear, with a visual tag (gray coat, gloves, van). They are the series spine.

evidence.note: Recruits you.
Moves in frozen time.
Guilty phone call, dossiers, accused.

characters.reuse: Create our own recurring figure with a unique visual tag (do not copy the gray coat). Show more ambiguity each episode: help, then a secret, then a lie.

characters.name: Ensemble cameo roll-call
characters.description: Heroes from earlier episodes appear with one visual tag (hoodie colour, goggles, headphones, home-made armour, cap) and one gag line each. The audience gets callbacks; the new hero learns where they stand in the team.

evidence.note: Five members, each with one gag.
Includes the previous episode's hero.

characters.reuse: Keep a cast bible with each past hero's tag and tic. Use at most 5 roll-call lines in 60-75 s.

characters.name: On-the-ground antagonist
characters.description: A peer bully (the trigger for the moral slide) or a villain pair whose powers counter the team (a touch-copier plus a time-stopper).

evidence.note: Bully triggers revenge.
Touch-copier and time-stopper pair.

characters.reuse: A villain's power should counter the hero's specific rule (a copier counters touch; a time-stopper counters speed).

characters.name: Love interest: absent (gap)
characters.description: None of the 3 uses romance. In the neighbouring motivational niche, adding a love counterpart was the biggest multiplier (LUST VS LOVE at 19.5x the channel median, per docs/research/script_analysis.md).

evidence.note: No romantic subplot in 8,000+ narrated words.

characters.reuse: Optional differentiator: a crush as witness or innocent, kept light and age-appropriate (no kissing, no jealousy plots). Test it in 1 of 5 episodes.

set_pieces.name: Precision rescue (the power is the danger)
set_pieces.description: The power used at full strength would hurt the person you save, so the rescue needs restraint, maths and the planted rule. The kid is saved, an object is not.

evidence.note: Arriving at full speed would be like a car hitting him, so you brake from exactly the planted distance.

set_pieces.reuse: Ask how the power would hurt someone it touches, then build the rescue around a controlled, rule-based version. Lose a symbolic object as the small price.

set_pieces.name: Frozen tableau
set_pieces.description: A world held still (ball mid-spiral, fireworks pressed in the sky, a tyre mid-air) for awe and dread. These beats have the lowest cut rate in Shapeshift (4.7 cuts/min): long held wides and slow camera walks through still crowds.

evidence.note: Frozen stadium.
Frozen crash on the highway.

set_pieces.reuse: Cheap and spectacular in our engine: freeze actors and FX at a keyframe and dolly the camera. Use 1 per episode, 15-30 s, with 2-4 long shots.

set_pieces.name: Temptation heist
set_pieces.description: A planned crime with a clean method (frozen cameras), interrupted by an innocent in danger. The choice is the set piece.

evidence.note: Cash truck on the overpass.

set_pieces.reuse: Use it for anti-hero episodes. The method should be clever and rule-based, and the interruption should mirror an early kindness.

set_pieces.name: Infiltration in disguise
set_pieces.description: The hero hides inside the enemy space, one near-miss shows the danger of discovery, and the hero comes to sympathise with the people being spied on.

evidence.note: A month as an equipment case.

set_pieces.reuse: Works with any stealth power. Include a near-miss (a sense the power can't fool) and a moment where the hero learns the enemy is likeable.

set_pieces.name: Arena ensemble battle as a chain of rule payoffs
set_pieces.description: In a big public arena, each team member lands one signature move. The hero survives a series of attacks by applying each planted rule in turn (weight, study, flatness).

evidence.note: Goalpost, jersey pile, mascot, tarp.

set_pieces.reuse: For 12-min episodes or longer. List the attacks first, then assign each a rule from the episode. Never solve one with a rule that wasn't planted.

set_pieces.name: Try-fail comic crash
set_pieces.description: A low-stakes failure that teaches the limit physically (missing a turn and ending up in a pool; stuck as a laundry basket). It sits in Act 1-2 and is played for comedy.

evidence.note: Hedge, two backyards, then a pool.
No legs, only a lid.

set_pieces.reuse: Use 1-2 per episode. The crash must visibly demonstrate the number just stated.

set_pieces.name: Power flex walk-through
set_pieces.description: In the last minute the hero shows total control (walks between frozen opponents, flicks the can), and then a reversal breaks it.

evidence.note: Hubris just before the reversal.

set_pieces.reuse: Put pride before the cliffhanger: a 10-20 s flex, then the rule breaks.

set_pieces.name: Cut density by beat type
set_pieces.description: Comedy montages are the fastest-cut beats (10x Faster cold open 43.6 cuts/min, perks 27.7; Stop Time misuse 38, proof test 36.9). Explainer beats with navy cards are slower (8-15). Big set pieces are held longer (Shapeshift stadium 2.5-12 cuts/min). Spectacle comes from scale and stillness, not cutting.

evidence.note: Computed from shot detection.

set_pieces.reuse: Plan 25-40 cuts/min for gags and montages, 10-18 for explainers and dialogue, and 5-12 for set pieces (long moves, wides).

comedy.name: Deadpan two-beat
comedy.description: A short claim, then a shorter contradiction or confirmation, often 2-4 words each. The most reused rhythm in the corpus.

evidence.note: The silly fix that works.

comedy.reuse: Use after every workaround and after every big claim. Write fresh pairs; never reuse corpus pairs.

comedy.name: Witness quip of 8 words or fewer
comedy.description: Character lines are short reactions, not exposition. 8-12% of words are dialogue, with a line every 19-25 s.

evidence.note: 10x Faster: 32 lines in 10:19. Stop Time: 24. Shapeshift: 55 in 22:06.

comedy.reuse: Aim for 25-32 character lines per 10 min, almost all 8 words or fewer. Exposition stays in the narrator's voice.

comedy.name: Narrator aside to the viewer
comedy.description: The narrator briefly talks to the viewer: answers the question the viewer is about to ask (no sonic boom), tells them not to try something, or winks about morality.

evidence.note: Answers the viewer's obvious question.
Gross-out warning; you were never promised to be the hero.

comedy.reuse: Use 1-3 per episode, each under 10 words, best placed right after a perk.

comedy.name: List of three, twist on the last
comedy.description: Three items, with the third breaking the pattern (escalating, absurd or self-aware).

evidence.note: Chores; breakfast counting.
Places the mug turns up.

comedy.reuse: Item 3 should be the longest or the most absurd. Use 3-5 per episode.

comedy.name: Literal physics gag
comedy.description: A rule taken literally produces an absurd image: a 50-kg pigeon, a couch snapping, the ball left at midfield, getting soaked by frozen rain, a water fountain running down the hall.

evidence.note: Couch, pigeon.
Frozen rain.

comedy.reuse: For every rule, ask what single image shows it taken to the extreme. That image is the gag and the shot.

comedy.name: Gamer or anime reference from the friend
comedy.description: One pop-culture label per episode, said by a peer (a running style, a speedrun term, an anime time-stop). It grounds the teen register and shows the audience how to describe the power.

evidence.note: Running style, speedrun route.
Anime time-stop.

comedy.reuse: Use 1-2 per episode, from the friend only, and never as the punchline of an emotional beat. Pick references a 13-20-year-old knows.

comedy.name: Running gag with late payoff
comedy.description: A tiny object gag is planted early and pays off in the last act or the final scene (cereal, peanut-butter bars, the coffee mug).

evidence.note: Cereal.
Peanut-butter bars.

comedy.reuse: Use one running gag per episode with 2-3 appearances. Its final appearance should come right before or after the most serious beat.

comedy.name: Laugh, then silence
comedy.description: A comic exchange followed by a flat statement that nobody laughs, which turns the scene serious within one sentence.

evidence.note: Jokes land, nobody laughs, then the mentor's stare.

comedy.reuse: Use it before the cliffhanger to switch tone sharply.

comedy.name: Understatement in danger
comedy.description: After a high-stakes beat, a dry understatement (the ball didn't make it; 'you're welcome') releases the tension.

evidence.note: The ball is the casualty.

comedy.reuse: Use one per climax. It must be about an object, never about a person getting hurt.

numbers.name: Number density tracks performance
numbers.description: The most-viewed video has 6x the numeric density of the second (3.8 vs 0.6 numeric tokens/min). Numbers make the fantasy feel engineered and give viewers comment ammunition.

evidence.note: 39 numbers in 10 min.

numbers.frequency: correlation in n=3; treat as a hint
numbers.reuse: Target 2-4 numbers per minute in the first half and 1 per minute in the second. Every number needs a picture (card or overlay).

numbers.name: Normal vs you pairs
numbers.description: Each key number comes as a pair: an ordinary baseline and your value.

evidence.note: 4 kg cat vs 50 kg you; 6 million vs 300 million smell sensors.

numbers.reuse: Never state a lone number. Pair it with the human baseline or a world record.

numbers.name: One-breath worked maths
numbers.description: Rate x amount = result, then conversion into a familiar unit, in 2-4 sentences. Viewers feel smart and the cost feels inevitable.

evidence.note: 1 kcal per kg per km x 70 kg x 200 km.
1 h/day = about 2 extra weeks a year.

numbers.reuse: Use 2-3 worked sums per episode. Check the arithmetic. Show the sum on a navy card (stat or compare).

numbers.name: Familiar-unit conversion
numbers.description: Big numbers become everyday objects: three football fields, a category 5 hurricane, faster than a highway car, a week of food every day, cereal boxes the size of an appliance.

evidence.note: Hurricane; football fields.

numbers.reuse: Every number of 3 or more digits gets one familiar unit, preferably something teens see daily (school bus, phone, football pitch, pizza).

numbers.name: Tiny number, huge consequence
numbers.description: A microscopic quantity with a dramatic everyday effect (microseconds of clock drift become kilometres of map error).

evidence.note: GPS relativity.

numbers.reuse: Use it in the science anchor when the power is subtle (time, perception, luck).

numbers.name: Counted stakes
numbers.description: The crowd or the danger is counted and the count is repeated, to build dread.

evidence.note: A seat count, then a hand count.

numbers.reuse: At the crisis, give one number for the scale of danger and repeat it in a new form.

retention.name: New information every 25-40 s
retention.description: Measured median gap between beats that add a new fact, rule, problem or plot information: 25 s, 31 s and 40 s. The longest dry spells (81-116 s) are inside emotional or action sequences, never inside explanation.

evidence.note: Computed per video.

retention.reuse: When outlining, mark each beat N (new information). No more than 40 s without an N in the first 60% of the runtime.

retention.name: Story turn every 80-120 s
retention.description: Turns (but-turn, real problem, crisis, dilemma, reversal, reveal, cliffhanger) come every 79-120 s in the 10-min episodes. That is a re-hook roughly every 1.5 minutes.
retention.reuse: Put a hard turn or open-loop re-hook at every 60-90 s mark (YouTube retention dips). Use the beat sheet times in STORY_BLUEPRINT.md.

retention.name: At least one open loop alive at all times
retention.description: From the planted limit at 0:22 to the cliffhanger, there is always an unresolved question. New loops open before old ones close (the ageing loop opens before the misuse loop; the folder loop opens before the stadium).

evidence.note: Plant-to-payoff spans of 2-15 minutes.

retention.reuse: Track loops on a timeline. When one closes, another must already be open.

retention.name: End every segment on a button
retention.description: Each beat ends on a short stinger: a quip, an ironic understatement, or an ominous half-line that pulls into the next beat.

evidence.note: A kindness flagged as the best use of the power.

retention.reuse: The last sentence of every beat is under 8 words and is a punchline, a reversal or a teaser.

retention.name: Cutaway to the watcher
retention.description: A brief cut to someone else watching the same footage. It creates dramatic irony and tees up the final act.

evidence.note: Someone in a van watches the same footage.

retention.reuse: Use one per episode, right after the public artefact (E6).

retention.name: Teaser before every fact
retention.description: See M2. Micro curiosity gaps keep the explainer sections watched.

evidence.note: 'Something weird' before the illusion fact.

retention.reuse: Every navy-card fact gets a teaser line.

endings.name: Ironic public reframe
endings.description: The climax becomes a public artefact whose name or caption states the theme ironically (a viral title, CCTV, a news line).

evidence.note: Viral clip named after the episode's irony.

endings.reuse: Name the clip or headline after the opposite of the power (a slow speedster, an unseen time-stopper).

endings.name: The bigger world knocks
endings.description: In the last 15-25%, the organisation physically arrives (knock, van, team waiting) with an offer or a threat.

evidence.note: Knock at night.
Van at dawn.

endings.reuse: Choose arrival, recruitment or confrontation depending on whether the hero did right (recruit) or wrong (confront).

endings.name: Fear in the strongest
endings.description: The final threat is shown by its effect on someone powerful (the mind-reader is scared, the time-stopper is not alone, the leader can't meet her team's eyes).

evidence.note: The mind-reader can't read the new threat.

endings.reuse: Introduce the next threat through a counter-rule: someone or something the established powers can't touch.

endings.name: Last-beat rule break
endings.description: The final story beat breaks a rule established in this episode (someone moves in frozen time; the trusted mentor is implicated).

evidence.note: Someone else is moving in a frozen world.

endings.reuse: Pick the rule the audience trusts most and break it in the last 20 s.

endings.name: Perspective flip across episodes
endings.description: The new episode reveals that its hero was the previous episode's mysterious threat.

evidence.note: The unreadable figure from the 10x Faster finale is you.

endings.reuse: Plan cliffhanger N to be episode N+1's hero. It is a cheap way to make sequels mandatory viewing.

endings.name: Family grounding before the leap
endings.description: Just before the cliffhanger, a parent gives a mundane blessing or worry. It keeps the hero a kid and makes the final threat feel bigger.

evidence.note: Mom with a spoon gives permission with a curfew.

endings.reuse: One family line inside the bigger-world beat.

cta.name: Two-question CTA
cta.description: In the last 16-22 s: Q1 is a personal fantasy (what would you do first with the power), Q2 is a story debate (who is the villain; join or fight; is she telling the truth). Then a comment ask, an 'only the beginning' line and the channel tagline.

evidence.note: Fantasy question, then a villain-identity question.
Fantasy question, then join or fight.
Three questions, the last about trust.

cta.reuse: Q2 must be answerable only by having watched the episode (it drives informed comments). Keep the CTA to 15-20 s. Write our own sign-off line.

cta.name: Description = provocation + debate + one link
cta.description: The description has a one-line provocation (the power sounds great until a specific catch, or challenges the viewer to be honest), the debate question, one related-episode link and a tagline.

evidence.note: Catch-line, villain question, link to another episode.
An honesty challenge.

cta.reuse: Write the provocation line before the script: if you can't write it, the cost isn't clear enough.

voice.name: Second person, present tense, concrete verbs
voice.description: 'You' is the protagonist throughout, in the present tense. Average sentence length is 8-9 words, with runs of 2-4-word sentences at action peaks and occasional 20+ word montage lists.

evidence.note: 8.9, 8.1 and 8.7 words.

voice.reuse: See the voice rules in STORY_BLUEPRINT.md section 6.

voice.name: Rhythm of repetition at action peaks
voice.description: Climaxes use word repetition to stretch time ('down and down and down', 'tap tap tap').

evidence.note: Sound and slow-down repetition.

voice.reuse: Use one repetition run per climax: 3 repetitions, with SFX on each.

visual.name: Navy explainer cards for every number
visual.description: Science and numbers move to a flat navy card with thin white line art, orange/gold accent numbers and ALL-CAPS labels (14,000 CALORIES, 14 METERS, 38 MICROSECONDS, a map grid with red corners, a stride diagram).

evidence.note: From the overview contact sheet.
Eye, clock and satellite cards.

visual.frequency: 2/3 heavily; Shapeshift instead puts science in 3D (reef, face wall)
visual.reuse: Our card types (stat, compare, distance, speed, clock, chain, rules, icon, title) map one-to-one. Each card is 3-6 s with one animated element.

visual.name: HUD overlays on 3D shots
visual.description: Numbers are also overlaid on live 3D shots: a speedometer gauge going from 25 to 250 km/h on the track, a '10X' label on the sprint, 'RULE 3' over the court.

evidence.note: Hook sheet: gauge and 10X label.
RULE 3 label.

visual.reuse: Use a StatCallout or gauge overlay when the number belongs to an action happening in 3D, and a navy card when it is abstract.

visual.name: Title card in-world
visual.description: The title text is composited over a 3D establishing shot of the episode's world, never on a blank card.

evidence.note: Aerial suburb.
Wall clock.

visual.reuse: Use the 'title' card type as an overlay on a wide of the main set.

visual.name: Letterbox for the epic
visual.description: The 22-min episode is letterboxed (about 2.35:1 bars) throughout, which signals a 'movie'. The 10-min ones are full-frame 16:9.

evidence.note: Visible in the contact sheets.

visual.reuse: Reserve letterbox for finales or 15+ min specials.
